turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, sit yourself down. The appendix came out ten days ago, yeah?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, ten days. Tuesday, I think. I don't know, doctor, the days are all muddled.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): What's brought you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The cut's gone red, and there's gunk coming out of it. It doesn't look right.
[SEG0005] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'm Pat, her carer, mornings and evenings. I took the dressing off before we left and the gauze was soaked.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soaked with what?
[SEG0007] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Yellow stuff. Thick. Smelt a bit off, too, not just like skin.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't think so. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the wound painful?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, we couldn't find a park on Johnston Street, that's why we were late. Sorry.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Forget the park. Is the wound sore?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh. Yeah, it stings if I twist, or getting up off the couch. Not screaming pain.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): What colour is that discharge?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I felt too crook to eat breakfast. Just tea.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): The colour. Of the stuff from the wound.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Yellow? Pat saw it properly, not me.
[SEG0018] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Definitely yellow. A bit green on the edge of the pad, but mostly yellow.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long's the redness been there?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): About a week? I don't know. Maybe I saw it and just ignored it.
[SEG0021] person_3 (CAREGIVER): It wasn't red when I dressed it Friday. I'd say three days, not a week.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between three days and a week. You're not matching.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Could be either.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any vomiting?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diarrhoea?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bowels have been a bit slow, but no runs.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any trouble passing urine?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough? Short of breath?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Neither.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diabetes?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Not that I know of.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Allergies to any medicines?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which antibiotic did the hospital send you home on?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, Keflex. Those capsules. Two hundred and fifty... no, five hundred milligrams, three times a day.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days' worth?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days... or was it seven? I don't know, doctor. I can't even remember what day I started them.
[SEG0040] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Bottle's at home. I wasn't there when they discharged her.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you actually been taking them?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly. I might've missed a couple of mornings. I don't know. Mornings are a blur.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): And for pain?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Panadol. Two of the five-hundred ones, when it stings. Not on a schedule.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else? Blood thinners?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just those.
[SEG0047] person_3 (CAREGIVER): She was shivering last night, doctor. Teeth chattering. I nearly rang someone.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): You told me no fever.

[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, yeah, I forgot. I was freezing and then boiling. Pat did the thermometer and it said thirty-eight point nine... no, thirty-eight point four. I don't know why I said no.
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Last night only?
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Just last night. I feel warm today, but not shaky.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Numbers first, then I'll look. Lie back for me.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Temp now is thirty-seven point six, and the pulse was one hundred and four... no, ninety-four. Blood pressure's one-thirty over eighty-two. Oxygen's ninety-seven percent, breathing sixteen.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wound's red for about five centimetres around the stitches, warm, and there's yellow pus at the lower end. Tender there. The wound itself hasn't opened up. Tummy's soft away from that.
[SEG0055] person_3 (CAREGIVER): That's the same stuff that was on the dressing. More than yesterday, I reckon.
[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): This looks like a wound infection. I won't know the bug until we swab it.
[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to go back into hospital? I don't know, doctor, I really don't want that.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. You're not crashing. I'll swab the wound and send bloods, a full blood count and a CRP.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stop the Keflex. I'm switching you to flucloxacillin, five hundred milligrams, four times a day, for seven days. By mouth.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Four times? I'll forget. I already muck up the other one.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Set an alarm. Take it on an empty stomach, an hour before food. Finish the seven days even if it looks better.
[SEG0062] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I can do the morning and the evening ones when I'm there. She'll have to manage the other two.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep it covered with a clean dry dressing, change it daily, and wash your hands first.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the redness takes off, the fever comes back, you start vomiting, or you feel faint, go straight to emergency. Don't sit on it.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Otherwise I'll see you back here in two days, sooner if you're worse.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Two days. Okay. I don't know if the chemist will even have it.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): They will. Script's electronic. Reception'll book the two days, and we're finished.

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

omissions.text: Caregiver reported the wound discharge was thick and smelt unpleasant/off; discharge was also described as a bit green at the edge of the dressing pad, not just yellow.
Patient initially denied fever, then corrected this: last night she was freezing then boiling, with shivering/teeth chattering; she feels warm today but not shaky.
Current cephalexin/Keflex use is recorded as currently used, but the doctor told her to stop Keflex and switch antibiotics.
Cephalexin adherence detail missing from medication record: patient had been taking it only 'mostly' and may have missed a couple of morning doses.
Paracetamol/Panadol dose is incompletely recorded: she takes two 500 mg tablets when it stings (i.e. 1000 mg per dose), not a single 500 mg dose.
Doctor documented that the patient was not acutely unstable: 'Not today. You're not crashing,' in response to whether hospital admission was needed.
Caregiver stated the wound drainage was more than yesterday.
Follow-up plan included returning sooner than two days if worse.
